title: The gurdwaras left behind
hookLine: a prayer for free access to Nankana Sahib and the gurdwaras across the border

lines: A WHITE BUILDING ACROSS THE FIELDS.
cards: On the Indian side of the border in Punjab, near the town of Dera Baba Nanak, there's a viewing platform.

For years, people climbed it with binoculars to look across a few miles of fields at a white building on the other side. They couldn't go there. They just looked, sometimes for a long time, and some of them wept.
The building was Gurdwara Kartarpur Sahib, where Guru Nanak spent his last years and died. It's in Pakistan now. And every day, all over the world, the Ardas asks for a door to open.

teach.b: At Partition, when British India was divided into India and Pakistan, the new border ran straight through Punjab.

The violence of that year fell on Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs alike; huge numbers were killed and uprooted on both sides. Sikh families who had lived in western Punjab for generations left everything and moved east.

They left behind places at the heart of Sikh history: Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born; Kartarpur, where he farmed and died; Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal; Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore, where Guru Arjan was martyred; and many more.

After Partition, a new line entered the Ardas. In paraphrase: grant the Khalsa open access to see, serve and care for Sri Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras and holy places from which the Panth has been separated.

teach.h: VICHHORA: THE ACHE OF BEING PARTED.
teach.b: The word for that separation is vichhora, the ache of being parted from someone you love. It's the same word Gurbani uses for the soul parted from God. Look at what it asks.
Not ownership. Not conquest. Khulhe darshan deedaar: to see them freely.

teach.h: TO SEE AND SERVE, NOT TO OWN.
teach.b: And sevaa sambhaal: to serve and look after them. For decades, Sikh pilgrims have crossed in groups for the great festivals, with permission from both governments.
More recently, a corridor opened that let pilgrims from India walk to Kartarpur Sahib for the day, though whether it is open has depended on relations between the two countries.
Some of the people on that viewing platform finally went. The prayer is still said, every day, for the rest.

how: Since Partition, the Ardas has asked for open access to Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras in Pakistan; Sikh pilgrims cross for major festivals, and the Kartarpur corridor has at times allowed day visits from India.

o: a border line drawn between two countries
a journey of pilgrims to a holy place
the ache of being parted from what you love

games.q: the gurdwaras left behind — tap the pairs.

s: this line has been in the Ardas since the time of the Gurus
the prayer asks for ownership of the gurdwaras
it asks to see, serve and care for them freely.
Kartarpur Sahib is where Guru Nanak spent his last years
it lies across the border, in Pakistan now.

games.q: you're on the viewing platform near Dera Baba Nanak, looking across at Kartarpur Sahib. what does the Ardas ask for?
o: open access to see and serve the gurdwaras left behind.
that people forget and move on.
games.why: khulhe darshan deedaar te sevaa sambhaal: to see them freely and to care for them. later, a corridor to Kartarpur Sahib opened.

practice: If you can, face west, toward Nankana Sahib from Indian Punjab; if not, picture a horizon.

Think of a place you can't go back to, a childhood home, a town, a country, and let yourself feel the vichhora, the ache of it, without hurrying it away. If you pray, say Waheguru toward that horizon.

wordCard.voice: Vichhora, the ache of being parted from a place or person you love: the Ardas asks to see and serve freely the holy places across the border, Nankana Sahib and Kartarpur among them.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vichhora, separation, the ache of being parted; used in Gurbani for the soul parted from God.

carryVoice: Your line: doors left behind. Not to own them: to see them freely, and to serve. Rest well.
